clocks.label: SCO BISHKEK
clocks.why: Putin, Xi and Modi meet for the bloc's 25th-anniversary summit. It prices the Russia-China file: whether Moscow's deepening dependence buys Beijing anything nameable, or whether the communique is again a photograph of a partnership that agrees on nothing operational.

clocks.label: G20 ASHEVILLE
clocks.why: Bessent hosts G20 finance ministers on US soil after skipping the South Africa process, demanding members sever business ties with Iran. This clock prices GEO-010 and GEO-011: whether the sanctions siege gets multilateral cover or stays a unilateral instrument other governments quietly route around.

clocks.label: XI SUMMIT
clocks.why: The state visit that GEO-006 (85%) and GEO-012 (31%) both hang on. If a Hormuz concession appears only in the thirty days AFTER it, the leverage-play read is confirmed; if it appears before, the read is wrong.

clocks.label: RU FUEL EXPORT BAN
clocks.why: Moscow's ban on most diesel, gasoline and jet exports, first imposed July 8 and now weighed for a second extension. Each extension is a public admission of how much refining Ukraine's drones have taken offline - and it removes product from a world market where Hormuz is still restricted.

clocks.label: IRAN-OMAN WINDOW
clocks.why: The 30-60 day technical-talks clock from the Muscat corridor framework. If it lapses with no verified minesweeping calendar and no corridor coordinates, the sixth near-breakthrough-then-condition cycle completes and the nobody-is-hurrying read on Hormuz strengthens.

clocks.label: US MIDTERMS
clocks.why: The master clock every captured file is priced against. Pump prices, casualties and endless-war branding all bill on this date - it is why not-in-a-hurry is the posture, and why a visible retreat before it is the falsifier on the coalition-capture hypothesis.

speculation.obs: gCaptain, working from Kpler and Vortexa vessel-tracking data, reported that just two commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Monday 24 August - one very large gas carrier and one very large crude carrier - the lowest daily tally since early May, against a ten-day average of 14 and seven vessels of all types the day before. Vortexa put that day’s oil transit at about 5 million barrels a day against a seven-day moving average of 6 to 7 million as of 23 August.
speculation.src: gCaptain, 25 Aug 2026, citing Kpler and Vortexa ship-tracking data; Vortexa analyst Xavier Tang quoted
speculation.read: Labelled inference, not fact: two hulls in a day is not a corridor, it is a formality. If the counts hold, the useful thing they establish is a floor rather than a trend - a number low enough that it can be moved by a single convoy decision, which means transit tallies are now measuring escort policy more than they measure demand. That matters for reading any announcement of reopening: a jump from two to twenty would tell you the US Navy changed a rule, not that Iran changed its mind. It is also the denominator against which this weekend’s exchange of fire should be judged.
speculation.falsifier: A sustained run of daily transits back into double digits, with oil throughput above 7 million barrels a day, would mean the escort arrangement is functioning and the floor was temporary. Continued single-digit days through September confirms the corridor is nominal.

speculation.obs: Maritime-intelligence firm Windward reported that all three loading terminals at Kharg Island - the terminal through which the overwhelming majority of Iranian crude normally leaves - had been empty for extended runs as of 9 August: the western terminal for 22 consecutive days since 18 July, the LPG terminal for 13 days since 27 July, the eastern terminal for 10 days since 30 July. Vortexa recorded zero departures between 31 July and 9 August, and the waiting area held 17 stationary tankers with their AIS transponders off.
speculation.src: Windward Maritime AI blog, 9 Aug 2026, with Vortexa departure data
speculation.read: Labelled inference: an empty berth is one of the few facts in this theatre that cannot be announced away, because a jetty either has a hull alongside it or it does not. If the run of empty days is right, the interesting number is not the shortfall but the 17 dark tankers parked outside it - that is loaded-and-waiting capacity, or capacity waiting to load, sitting where a satellite can count it. Iran’s export halt would then be a queue rather than a collapse, which matters because a queue clears in days once a corridor opens and a collapse does not. Treat the three-week age of this observation as the main caveat; it is a baseline, not today.
speculation.falsifier: Fresh imagery or Vortexa data showing hulls back alongside the Kharg terminals, with departures resuming, would date-stamp the halt as over. Terminals still empty into September, with the dark waiting-area count rising, would mean the storage-afloat problem is compounding.

speculation.obs: Windward tracked eight sanctioned Russian shadow-fleet tankers moving as a coordinated convoy through the Northern Sea Route toward the Laptev Sea in late July and early August - four Russia-flagged Aframaxes, three Russia-flagged Medium Range tankers and one Oman-flagged Suezmax - loaded at Murmansk and Primorsk between 13 and 22 July with cargoes of roughly 700,000 to 1 million barrels each, several signalling China as destination. The Center for High North Logistics recorded 34 tankers using the route in all of 2025.
speculation.src: Windward Maritime AI blog, 9 Aug 2026; route baseline from the Center for High North Logistics
speculation.read: Labelled inference: eight hulls in one convoy against a 34-hull annual baseline is not a shipping story, it is a routing decision. If the count holds, Russia is testing whether the Arctic can carry sanctioned barrels to Asia outside the insurance, chokepoint and inspection regimes that police the Baltic and Suez routes - a lane with no Danish strait to be boarded in and no Hormuz to be closed. That is the physical fact sitting underneath Lavrov’s complaint today that NATO activity in the Arctic is a direct threat to Russia: the alliance is moving into the region where Moscow is building its sanctions bypass, and the ice window that makes the bypass usable is only a few weeks long.
speculation.falsifier: A second convoy of comparable size before the ice window closes in October, or Chinese customs data showing Arctic-routed Russian crude arriving, would confirm the lane is being industrialised. A single passage with no repeat, or the convoy dispersing short of the Laptev, would mean it was an experiment.

speculation.obs: Open-source imagery analyst MenchOsint posted a Sentinel-2 satellite frame dated 27 August 2026 showing a Kuwaiti Aframax oil tanker sitting idle in the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz after being struck by the IRGC Navy, with a second, smaller boat alongside it - read by the analyst as an attempt to take off the crew. UKMTO had reported a tanker disabled by an attack in the strait on the evening of 26 August, and the incident was picked up by trade press.
speculation.src: @MenchOsint on X (Sentinel-2 imagery); underlying strike reported by UKMTO and Seatrade Maritime
speculation.read: Labelled inference, not fact: the strike itself is corroborated by UKMTO and trade press, so what the imagery adds is the aftermath - a hull still afloat and stationary in the southern channel a day later, with a boat alongside. If that read holds, the IRGC is disabling rather than sinking, and those are different campaigns. A disabled tanker parked in a traffic lane is a durable advertisement that the corridor is conditional, and it costs Tehran far less in escalation than a hull on the bottom. The duller alternative is simply that the weapon underperformed. Either way this is the class of evidence that matters most while transponders are unreliable, because a satellite does not care whether AIS is switched on.
speculation.falsifier: Salvage or a tow, plus an owner or flag-state statement putting damage at the low end, fits the disable-not-sink read. A subsequent strike that actually sinks a hull, or evidence the vessel was simply anchored and undamaged, would break it.

speculation.obs: C4ADS published an ADS-B audit of Russian state and state-linked air traffic into the central Sahel: 75 military or military-linked flights between 1 January 2025 and 31 July 2026, with Burkina Faso used as the intermediate hub, Mali next, and Niger receiving only six. The busiest operator was Flight Unit 224, a Russian defence-ministry airline sanctioned by the US in 2023; the aircraft were mostly Il-76TDs. C4ADS also places the Africa Corps operation at Airbase 101 in Niamey, the field US forces used until their 2024 withdrawal.
speculation.src: C4ADS, ‘Routes and Ramifications’, published 12 Aug 2026 (FlightRadar24 ADS-B data)
speculation.read: Labelled inference, not fact - and this weekend put it to the test. Six flights in nineteen months is a thin pipe, yet the detachment at the end of it is what Niamey’s base command called when its own soldiers mutinied. If the count is right, the Russian presence that just decided a mutiny is supplied overland through Burkina Faso rather than by a dedicated air bridge into Niger. That cuts two ways and we still do not know which. A small advisory detachment that can hold a capital is cheaper leverage than a garrison and easier to deny; but a guarantor that has now been publicly asked to fight has to start flying, and airlift is the one thing ADS-B makes visible in near-real time. This is the pre-crisis baseline the next month gets measured against.
speculation.falsifier: A visible burst of Flight Unit 224 or Il-76TD movements into Niamey over the next month, above the six-flight run rate, would mark the shift from advisers to garrison. Flat traffic while the junta still holds power would mean the assistance was small, local and mostly political.

quiz.q: Russia's defence ministry says its planned strikes on Ukraine's grid are retaliation for Kyiv's drone campaign. What has that Ukrainian campaign actually done to Russia?
options: Cut Russian crude production to its lowest level since the Soviet collapse
Pushed Russian refinery runs to a 24-year low and forced a ban on most fuel exports
Destroyed the pipelines carrying Russian crude to China
Halted Russian oil revenue almost entirely
quiz.why: The target is refining, not production. Russian refinery runs fell to roughly 3.6m barrels a day in July, the lowest since May 2002, and Moscow banned most diesel, gasoline and jet exports from July 8 to keep its own pumps supplied. Crude keeps flowing; the ability to turn it into fuel is what is being taken away.

quiz.q: Treasury moved against Banque Misr's UAE branches rather than a Chinese state bank. What does that choice suggest about the sanctions strategy?
options: Chinese banks have no exposure to Iranian oil trade
Egypt is a larger conduit for Iranian oil than China is
The expensive target is being deliberately spared while the instrument is demonstrated on a cheap one
The Treasury lacks legal authority over Chinese institutions
quiz.why: Banque Misr sits in a G20 member with little capacity to retaliate; China is the buyer that would actually decide the outcome and has been left untouched. An enforcer that repeatedly picks the cheapest available nail is telling you which nail it does not intend to hit - which is why the forecast on a Chinese bank designation went down, not up.

quiz.q: Why does the brief treat Mojtaba Khamenei's WRITTEN Islamic Unity Week message as meaningful evidence rather than routine?
options: Written messages are forbidden for a Supreme Leader on religious occasions
The occasion is the one his father delivered live for over three decades, so the medium was a conspicuous choice
It contained a new threat against the Gulf states
It was the first communication from him in six months
quiz.why: The information is in the missed focal occasion. If the Leader is a legitimacy token the IRGC holds rather than an operating ruler, handlers avoid live exposure exactly when it is most expected - so a text post at the highest-salience clerical moment of the year carries more signal than another quiet day would.

quiz.q: What makes the Pacific Islands Forum in Palau a useful gauge for China policy, despite its small size?
options: Its members control a chokepoint for global shipping
It is where diplomatic recognition is bought and sold one small state at a time, and where pressure that pauses can be told apart from pressure that ratchets
It has the authority to admit Taiwan to the United Nations
Its decisions bind Chinese fishing fleets
quiz.why: Recognition is retail in the Pacific: a switch costs one small state's decision and buys lasting maritime and diplomatic geometry. It is also a low-cost test of the harvest-cover hypothesis - whether Beijing's current softness is a pause bought for the September summit or a ratchet that keeps turning through it.

quiz.q: A headline reads: US declares the Strait of Hormuz cleared of Iranian mines. Which single observable would best tell you whether the strait has actually reopened?
options: A CENTCOM commander repeating the declaration on video
Published war-risk insurance premia falling back under 3% of hull value
Iran issuing a statement welcoming international shipping
Brent crude falling below $85
quiz.why: Underwriters, not commanders or ministries, price the reopening - they are paying real money on their own read of the risk and have no incentive to flatter anyone. The IMO secretary-general disputed the mine-free claim and the JMIC kept its severe rating, so the declaration and the insurance market disagree; the premium is the one that settles bets.

decode.claim: The United States has entered the biggest oil deal in history, taking majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil, more than doubling American oil reserves, substantially lowering gas prices, and at no cost to the American taxpayer.
decode.source: Trump social-media post, Aug 28; structure briefed by a US official
decode.verdictNote: Framing, and the load-bearing distinction is where reserves are counted. Oil reserves are booked to the ground they sit in, not to the nationality of the shareholder — 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan proven reserves stay Venezuelan reserves under every accounting convention, and what Washington describes buying is 55% of a new company's effective output, split between an equity stake and the right to buy barrels at cost. That is a claim on production, not title. “No cost to the American taxpayer” is also narrower than it sounds: it means no appropriated cash this year, not no sovereign risk on a 100-year concession under an interim government installed after the US removed its predecessor.
decode.reality: Trump announced the deal on social media on Aug 28 and named Marco Rubio, Pete Hegseth and Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodríguez as the negotiators. A US official describes a joint venture with a private Venezuelan company covering 17 fields, a 100-year lease over 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, and a 55% US share of effective output split between ownership and at-cost purchase rights, with at-cost barrels going to the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and the military. Venezuela is currently producing about 1.23m barrels a day — its highest since February 2019 — of which Chevron's joint venture accounts for roughly 260,000. For scale on the reserves claim: US proved crude and lease-condensate reserves were 46.4bn barrels at end-2023 (EIA), so 65bn is indeed the larger number, which is exactly why adding it across a border is the move worth catching.
decode.aspiration: No agreement text has been published. The private operator has not been officially named (reporting points to Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt). Nobody has said how the 55% divides between equity and at-cost rights, who funds the roughly $100bn of investment Rubio cited, or which sanctions authorisation lets a US government entity hold the stake. Venezuela's constitution treats hydrocarbons as inalienable public domain and no National Assembly ratification has been shown. Chevron and ExxonMobil both declined to comment — no major has committed capital. On prices: energy analysts Amy Myers Jaffe and Kevin Book both say the infrastructure work takes years and billions, and will not move the pump price this weekend.

angles.effect: Gains an energy-price story and a below-market SPR refill before the midterms, bought with an announcement rather than an appropriation — the cheapest possible instrument, and the reason it arrived as a post rather than a treaty.
Converts a transitional mandate into a governing one: recognition, sanctions relief and a promised $100bn of capital, paid for by pre-committing decades of the country's principal asset.

The concession runs through a private company, so operatorship of what a US official called the world's second-largest private oil company by reserves lands with one businessman rather than a state entity — while Chevron and Exxon pay nothing and say nothing, which is the correct position while the legal text, the sanctions carve-out and the arbitration clause are all missing.

angles.party: Venezuelans and any future elected government
angles.effect: Carry the bill. They inherit a contract they did not vote on, and a dilemma: honour it and a century of the resource is spoken for; break it and sanctions and the security question come straight back.

The party absent from the announcement. If Venezuelan heavy sour genuinely reaches Gulf refiners in volume, the Canadian heavy discount widens — Alberta pays part of the price of a Washington announcement and gets no seat in it.

clock.d90: Sentiment, not molecules. Production stays near 1.2–1.3m b/d and there is no measurable pump-price effect. The testable event is the signing session Caracas says is scheduled for next week, and whether a document appears with it.
clock.m18: The capital question resolves. Either an OFAC authorisation and a published contract exist and a major commits real money, or the deal stays a press release with a lease number attached. Watch whether output moves toward the stated 1.5m b/d.
clock.y7: Where 65bn either becomes barrels or does not. Orinoco extra-heavy crude needs upgraders, diluent, power and port capacity that do not exist at the claimed scale today — and this is also where political durability is tested, when a Venezuelan government that did not sign this has to decide whether to honour it.

watch: The published contract text — its governing law and arbitration seat, the legal name of the joint venture and the identity of the private operator. Its absence is currently the single biggest hole in the claim.
An OFAC general licence or amended sanctions authorisation covering the venture — without one, no US major can lawfully fund it.
A Venezuelan National Assembly ratification vote or gazette publication, given the constitution's inalienable-public-domain clause.
A first at-cost cargo delivered into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, with a dated bill of lading and the price paid versus market.
Venezuelan monthly production in OPEC secondary-source figures crossing 1.5m b/d.
decode.easy: The president said America now controls 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's oil, that it costs you nothing and that it will lower fuel prices. No signed contract has been published, the oil stays in Venezuelan ground under Venezuelan law, and getting it out takes years — so today this mostly helps the government in Caracas that needs the money and the private company that gets to run the fields.

decode.claim: Venezuela preserves ownership of and sovereignty over its resources under a 25-year agreement that returns $19 from every barrel sold to the US, worth up to $209 billion.
decode.source: Delcy Rodríguez, Venezuela's acting president, televised address
decode.verdictNote: Partly true, and the half that survives matters: Venezuela does keep legal title, because what Washington describes acquiring is a stake in a company plus purchase rights, not ownership of rock. Both governments can be telling the truth about that at the same time. What they cannot both be right about is the term — Caracas says 25 years, Washington says a 100-year lease — and the money does not reconcile either: 1.5m barrels a day at $19 a barrel is roughly $10bn a year, so $209bn is only reachable as a multi-decade cumulative total, not an annual one.
decode.reality: Rodríguez said in a televised address that the deal covers 17 strategic oilfields with an initial production target of 1.5m barrels a day plus eight greenfield blocks, that $19 from every barrel sold to the US flows to Caracas, and that Venezuela retains “ownership of and sovereignty” over its natural resources “while leveraging capital, technology and operational expertise.” She said agreements would be signed the following week. Venezuela's actual output today is about 1.23m b/d, with a government target of 1.37m by year-end — so 1.5m is an increase, not a transformation.
decode.aspiration: The 25-year term is asserted, not documented, and is directly contradicted by the US description of a 100-year lease. The $209bn figure, the $100bn of inbound investment, the eight greenfield blocks and the signing itself are all forward-looking. No text has been published, no National Assembly ratification has been reported, and the constitutional question — whether an inalienable public-domain resource can be committed this way at all — is untouched in her address.

angles.effect: Turns an interim mandate into a sovereignty-preserving national win and gets a fiscal number, $19 a barrel, that she can put in a budget speech. The word 'sovereignty' is doing the political work the term sheet cannot.

angles.party: The PSUV base and the Chavista tradition
angles.effect: Asked to accept foreign operatorship of the industry Chávez nationalised. 'Ownership retained' is the formula that makes that survivable inside the party — which is precisely why it was the first phrase in the address.
Boxed in. Opposing the deal means opposing sanctions relief and $100bn of investment; supporting it means blessing terms negotiated by a government seated after a US operation removed the last one.
Gains by conceding the word. Control of output was always the object, so letting Caracas keep the language of sovereignty costs nothing and stabilises the counterpart it needs to sign.

angles.party: Venezuelan citizens and every government after this one
angles.effect: Pay the spread. They receive $19 a barrel while the venture keeps the rest of the value chain, and they carry the difference between a 25-year commitment and a 100-year one — a gap of three generations that nobody has put in writing, agreed to by an unelected acting president on television.

clock.d90: The signing session Caracas promised. The only thing that matters is whether a stated term appears in a document — 25 or 100 — and whether the National Assembly touches it.
clock.m18: Whether $19-a-barrel receipts actually appear in Venezuelan fiscal accounts, and whether output moves from 1.23m toward the stated 1.5m b/d.
clock.y7: Whether the term survives a change of government in Caracas or of administration in Washington. A concession is paper until an institution enforces it.

watch: The stated term in the signed text — the one number that settles the 25-versus-100-year contradiction between the two announcing governments.
Whether the $19 per barrel is structured as royalty, tax or profit share, and whether it is indexed to price.
A National Assembly ratification vote or publication in the Gaceta Oficial.
A Venezuelan budget line showing receipts from the venture, in the next fiscal presentation.
Whether the eight greenfield blocks appear in the same instrument as the 17 producing fields or in a separate, later one.
decode.easy: Venezuela's acting president said the country keeps ownership of its oil, that the deal lasts 25 years and pays Venezuela $19 a barrel. The ownership part is fair — but Washington described the same deal as a 100-year lease, and the $209 billion she cited only works as a total over decades, not per year.

decode.claim: The violence in the West Bank villages of Qusra and Jalud was criminal, committed by a handful of rioters who are violating the law and harming Israel's standing in the world.
decode.verdictNote: The condemnation is real and unusually direct from this prime minister — but the load-bearing word is “handful,” which recasts a documented and recurring pattern as isolated deviance. The follow-through so far is evidentiary rather than prosecutorial: the military impounded vehicles for a police file, and no arrests were announced. Yesh Din's monitoring of 1,701 police investigations since 2005 finds 93.8% closed with no indictment and only 3% ending in conviction, so a statement and a case file are not the same object.
decode.reality: Dozens of settlers descended on Qusra on Saturday after nearly three weeks of tension, throwing stones at residents and barricading themselves inside a house with Palestinians still in it; in nearby Jalud settlers attacked a Palestinian family and an NBC News crew. The army removed settlers from the Palestinian home, separated the groups, and confiscated vehicles suspected of having been used to reach the area as evidence for a police investigation. Netanyahu's statement was issued the same day and is a rare rebuke.
decode.aspiration: Everything downstream of the words. No arrests were announced, no suspects named, no indictments filed, no administrative orders issued against Israeli citizens for these incidents. Nothing in the statement names an instrument — no policing change, no deadline, no minister tasked. Whether the impounded vehicles produce identified suspects is the open question, and the base rate says most such files close as “offender unknown”.

angles.effect: Buys international cover at zero coalition cost. Words carry no price with his partners; and note the injury he names is to 'the law-abiding Jewish community' and to 'Israel's standing in the world' — the framing is reputational, not about the people who were attacked.
Lose nothing. The statement stops precisely where a coalition fight would begin: it names no policy, no ministry and no enforcement target, so the national-security portfolio is untouched.

Handed an expectation without new authority or a deadline. The statement even describes the army as being 'interfered with' — casting the force responsible for order in the territory as the aggrieved party rather than the accountable one.

angles.party: Residents of Qusra and Jalud, and the reporters covering them
angles.effect: Pay in full and in advance. They face recurring attacks and a 93.8% no-indictment rate, which is the number that actually predicts their next year — not the sentence read out in Jerusalem. An NBC crew was attacked alongside them, and unpunished attacks on journalists mean fewer journalists in those villages, which erodes the evidence base condemnations depend on.

angles.party: European and US officials weighing settler sanctions
angles.effect: Handed the counter-argument. A prime-ministerial condemnation is the strongest available case for holding off on designations — which is a benefit to Israel's government whether or not a single indictment follows.

clock.d90: Whether the Qusra and Jalud files produce named suspects and indictments, or close. This is the only window in which the statement can be falsified cheaply.
clock.m18: Whether the 2026 indictment and conviction rates move off their twenty-year band. One prosecution is an anecdote; a shift in the percentage is a policy change.
clock.y7: Whether any enforcement architecture in Area C changes at all — jurisdiction, police staffing, or the standing of Israeli civilians under military versus civil law.

watch: A named indictment with a case number arising from the Qusra or Jalud incidents.
Whether the impounded vehicles yield identified suspects, or the files close on “offender unknown” — the disposition of those specific vehicles is the cheapest available test.
Any administrative detention or restraining order issued against Israeli citizens for these attacks.
Yesh Din's next data sheet and the 2026 closure and conviction percentages.
Whether the national security ministry publicly backs, contradicts or slow-walks the police investigation.
decode.easy: Israel's prime minister called the settler attacks on two Palestinian villages criminal, which he rarely does. But so far the army has only impounded some cars and nobody has been arrested — and over twenty years, 94 out of every 100 of these police files have closed with no charges at all.

decode.claim: The prompt reaction of Niger's defence and security forces contained the mutiny and gradually regained control of the sites attacked in Niamey.
decode.source: Niger junta statement read on state television
decode.verdictNote: Partly true — and the tell is inside the wording. A government that held its capital does not need to announce that it “gradually regained control” of sensitive sites; the sentence concedes the sites were lost before it claims they were recovered. Containment itself looks real — the state broadcaster came back on air, and the presidential guard repelled an attempt on the palace — but a diplomatic source told AFP the guard retook the air base “with the help of the Russians,” which, if confirmed, means the regime's own forces were not sufficient. That is the part of the day that has consequences, and it is not in the statement.
decode.reality: Sustained gunfire and explosions were reported on Aug 29 around Base 101, the presidential palace and the state broadcaster in Niamey. Soldiers from the Base 101 barracks opened fire on several sensitive sites after attempting to detain fellow soldiers. Télé Sahel went off air for about an hour before being restored around 10:00. Security sources confirmed an attempted breach of the presidential palace was pushed back by the presidential guard. This is the latest challenge to Abdourahamane Tiani, who took power in the 2023 coup.
decode.aspiration: Almost every operational detail. No casualty figures, no confirmed arrests, no confirmation of airport status, no named plotters, and — the absence that matters most — no dated public appearance by Tiani himself. The Russian assistance rests on a single anonymous diplomatic source and has not been confirmed or denied by Niamey or Moscow. “Contained” is a claim about a moving situation made by the party with the strongest interest in it being over.

angles.effect: Survive the day and acquire a licence for a purge of the officer corps — the standard post-mutiny move, and the one that tells you how frightened they actually were. Watch the arrest list, not the statement.

angles.party: The mutineers, reported as junior officers
angles.effect: If they are named and tried publicly, the regime is confident. If the files stay sealed and the men disappear into detention, it is not — secrecy after a failed coup usually indicates the plot reached higher than the government wants known.

angles.party: Russia and its Africa Corps presence
angles.effect: If the air base really was retaken with Russian help, Moscow converts a security service into standing political leverage over Niamey — over uranium contracts, over basing, over what Niger can refuse later. Protection is the most expensive thing a weak government can accept, and France and the US, already expelled from their Niger bases, have no instrument left to compete for it.

angles.party: The Sahel alliance partners, Mali and Burkina Faso
angles.effect: A wobble in Niamey wobbles all three. Their juntas rest on the same arithmetic of junior officers with weapons and grievances, and each attempt raises the perceived odds for the next — as it does for the uranium buyers repricing supply risk who were consulted by nobody.

Pay in curfews, communications cuts and a security establishment that now has to watch itself as well as the jihadist insurgency in Tillabéri — attention diverted from the threat that actually kills them.

clock.d90: Arrests, a military tribunal, and a reshuffle of the general staff or the presidential guard command. Also whether Tiani appears in person, on a dated broadcast — the cheapest proof of control there is.
clock.m18: Whether the purge stabilises the army or seeds the next attempt, and whether any Russian role formalises into a written basing or training agreement.
clock.y7: The base rate governs. Niger has now seen repeated coups and attempts; a regime that survives by purging its officer corps tends to meet the same event again, and each round narrows the pool of officers it can trust.

watch: A published list of arrested officers and the convening of a military tribunal — names and ranks, not a numbered total.
Tiani appearing in person on state television, with a verifiable date.
An official Nigerien or Russian statement confirming or denying Russian participation at Base 101 — the single missing document that would change the read of the whole day.
Reopening of Diori Hamani international airport and a return to published flight schedules.
Changes to the command of the presidential guard or the army general staff in the next gazette.
decode.easy: Soldiers attacked the presidential palace and an air base in Niger's capital, and the government says it contained the mutiny and took the sites back. Saying you “gradually regained control” admits you lost them first — and a diplomatic source says Russian forces helped, which would mean the government now owes Moscow for its own survival.

track.note: Nothing has resolved yet, and we publish that rather than dress it up. All 22 forecasts were checked against their deadlines in the Aug 30 audit and against early resolution - the Brent band is the only one that can resolve early, on a single daily close outside 80-100, and Brent settled 88.29 mid-band. The first real score lands Sep 24, then the Xi summit and the Chinese-bank question on Oct 1. Every score appears here as it happens, the misses first. A track record you can only see after it looks good is not a track record.

plumbing.read: The buffer is gone and the pressure is now in two places at once. ON RRP sits at $0.17B, down 84% on the month - the reverse-repo parking lot that would absorb any drain of short-end support is effectively empty - while the Fed balance sheet quietly expanded 0.8% to $6.73T. On the physical side, the product market is tightening from both ends: Russian refinery runs at a 24-year low with a fuel export ban running past Sept 1, and Hormuz still moving roughly a tenth of its pre-war traffic. What is still NOT printing is the milkshake tape - oil AND dollar expensive together. The broad dollar is soft at 118.1, down 2.4% on the month, and that remains the strongest live evidence against escalation. Pressure in the plumbing, not yet in the price.
plumbing.epoch: E6 still open — the Sept-2019 repo confession never closed — running alongside E7, the weaponized-settlement rail opened by the 2022 reserve freeze that the record official gold bid is a late chapter of.

series.note: the short end the Fed is buying

easy.bottomLine: America bombed a small Iranian island in the world’s most important shipping lane, and Iran fired missiles back at two American bases in Jordan. Almost all of those missiles were shot down and no Americans were killed, which usually means both sides want to stop rather than keep going. The bigger change overnight was about money: America’s top central banker hinted interest rates may go UP, the dollar got stronger, and oil got more expensive at the same time. hypotheses.name: NEW · Venezuela was a Hormuz hedge in a drug-war uniform
hypotheses.d: The clearest revealed-preference play on the board — and the reason it opens at 55 rather than higher. Sturdy mechanism first: US Gulf-Coast refineries are plumbed for heavy sour crude, Venezuela sits on the planet's largest heavy reserves, and moving that barrel north through the Caribbean to Texas and Louisiana structurally hedges the one risk that ran live all year — a Hormuz closure. The Aug 28-29 deal (a new operator taking control of ~65bn barrels, about a fifth of Venezuela's reserves) is exactly what this hypothesis predicts, and the reporting frames it in plain words as an alternative to Gulf oil routed through Hormuz. So oil-as-motive is near-certain. What is NOT settled — and what caps this — is premeditation: was Operation Southern Spear a counter-narcotics and regime-change campaign that harvested the oil after the fact, or an oil-security operation in a drug-war uniform from the start? The tell against design is the clock — the deal trailed Maduro's Jan 3 capture by eight months, which reads more like spoils than master plan. Mundane alternative, named and live: drugs, migration politics, regime-change, with the barrel a bonus. Falsifiers — cut hard if export volumes stay token (the $2-2.8bn tranches are a rounding error against control of 65bn bbl), if Gulf-Coast heavy sourcing does not actually swing off the Middle East, or if the fixed infrastructure (GEO-022) never appears. One correction the excitement needs: a canal cannot bypass Hormuz, geography does not work that way — the hedge is source substitution plus Caribbean routing, not a waterway. Real Orinoco or Maracaibo channel-dredging and dedicated heavy-crude terminals WOULD be the premeditation tell. Unconfirmed today; it is the thing to watch.

brief.h: Iran answered the Larak strike with ballistic missiles at two US bases in Jordan - and the load-bearing fact is that nearly all of them were intercepted
brief.t: Hours after US forces struck two IRGC launchers on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz - the first known American strike on Iran since late July, ordered after Revolutionary Guards were observed preparing to fire rockets carrying sea mines into the international lanes - the IRGC Aerospace Force fired ballistic missiles at two US bases in Jordan. The IRGC said the Larak strike killed and wounded Iranian fighters and civilians. Nearly all of the incoming was intercepted and no American deaths have been confirmed. Brent rose close to 2 percent.
brief.context: Name the mechanism: the advertised volley. There is a well-worn move on this file, and Al Asad in January 2020 is the reference case - a retaliation aimed at hardened, forewarned installations, sized to be survivable, is not a failed attack but a successful message. It buys the firing government proof of response for a domestic audience while buying the target government the option not to escalate, and its historical conversion rate into general war is low. The deciding desks here are CENTCOM and the IRGC Navy, not either capital’s podium. What makes the equilibrium fragile is not intent but arithmetic: interception is probabilistic, and one leaker into a barracks converts a message into a casualty event neither side can walk back. The other half of the board is minelaying, which is cheap, deniable and reversible - a cleared lane is a maintenance schedule, not a conquest, which is why the strike went at launchers on a rock rather than at anything strategic.

angles.effect: Gets a visible answer at near-zero cost and keeps the mine option, which is the actual leverage. An intercepted volley is retaliation Tehran can show at home without buying the war that killing Americans would start.
Demonstrates that “successfully cleared” is enforced rather than declared, and takes on the enforcement indefinitely. A lane you have to keep clearing is a standing commitment, not a victory.
Pays for hosting. Amman absorbs incoming ballistic missiles in a quarrel it is not party to and gains nothing it can show its own public.
Carry the bill. Brent near 90 dollars and US pump prices above 4 dollars a gallon, against under 3 when this began in late February, is the transfer actually being made.

dec.kill: Confirmed American deaths in Jordan or the strait, or a struck US hull, breaks the intercepted-volley equilibrium and this read with it. A fortnight with no further exchange and no fresh minelaying reported on the lanes would mean Sunday was maintenance rather than escalation.

brief.h: Warsh pushed September rate-HIKE odds to 57 percent, the yen went back through 160, and oil rose the same night - the two prices that are not supposed to climb together
brief.t: Fed chair Kevin Warsh said on Friday the central bank will “have work to do” if policymakers do not get the confidence they need that inflation is heading to 2 percent, his clearest signal yet that further tightening is live. Markets moved the implied probability of a September hike to 57 percent and the two-year Treasury to 4.33 percent, a more than one-month high. The dollar index held near 99.6, its strongest since 17 August, and the yen slipped to 160.01, back through the level widely read as raising intervention risk. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said recent yen moves had been “pretty well contained” and that he expected BOJ governor Kazuo Ueda to “do the right thing.” Brent rose nearly 2 percent after the Larak strike.
brief.context: Start with the constraint, not the character. Warsh is not hawkish by temperament this week; he is boxed by an oil shock arriving inside a CPI he has staked his credibility on defending, and a chair who concedes the 2 percent target during an energy spike gives up the only asset an inflation-fighting central bank owns. That is why the deciding desk is not the podium but the two-year note and the Bank of Japan’s bond desk. Name the mechanism: this is the milkshake configuration - oil and the dollar expensive at the same time - and it is the one combination that forces importing countries to sell reserves to afford both, because the barrel must be bought in a currency that is itself appreciating. Japan is the cleanest instance: it imports essentially all its crude, prices it in dollars, and now pays at 160 yen. The base rate on the yen is instructive - Tokyo has intervened around this level before, and intervention holds only when the rate gap is closing rather than widening, which is exactly what a hawkish Fed prevents.

angles.effect: Gains twice and pays once. A strong dollar cheapens the imported half of the oil shock and lets Bessent call the yen “contained” - but Treasury is also the borrower refinancing into a two-year at 4.33 percent, so the same hawkishness raises its own bill.

Pays the clearest price. A country importing every barrel in dollars at 160 yen is running an energy tax it never legislated, and its central bank is being told publicly from Washington what the right thing to do is.

angles.party: Dollar-indebted emerging markets and Gulf importers
angles.effect: Pay without a seat. They face the barrel and the currency in the same quarter, which is how an American inflation decision becomes somebody else’s reserve sale.

angles.party: US savers and the Fed’s credibility
angles.effect: Gain if the target holds. The case for the pain is that a defended 2 percent is worth more than a comfortable quarter, and that is a real argument rather than a fig leaf.

dec.kill: Confirmed Japanese intervention with a disclosed size, a BOJ hike, or a September CPI print soft enough to drop hike odds below about 25 percent would each break the “contained” framing. The yen through 165 with no intervention, or a hike actually delivered in September, confirms the read.

brief.h: Russia’s Africa Corps helped put down a mutiny at the Niamey airbase that houses its own headquarters - the field American forces left in 2024
brief.t: Soldiers mutinied at Base 101, the military airbase inside Niamey’s international airport, from Friday night into Saturday, with gunfire around the airport, the presidential palace and the state broadcaster. Reuters reported hundreds of soldiers involved but could not verify the figure; state media said dozens were killed or arrested. The mutineers reportedly included troops from Ouallam, Tera and Dosso, where the army has taken its heaviest losses to al-Qaeda- and ISIS-linked groups. Russia’s ambassador Viktor Voropaev confirmed base command requested help, and the Africa Corps - 200 to 300 personnel in Niger, under the Russian defence ministry - provided ground and aerial support. The presidential guard stayed loyal to General Abdourahamane Tiani, in power since July 2023.
brief.context: Name the mechanism: the regime-survival guarantee, and the invoice that comes with accepting one. The rail predates the headline - Base 101 is the field US forces used until the 2024 withdrawal, and Africa Corps headquarters now sits on it, so the mutineers seized the one location where the guarantor lives. The deciding desk is the Russian defence ministry rather than a deniable commercial contractor, which is what makes this a state commitment instead of a business. Our own watchtower supplies the base rate: C4ADS counted only six Russian military-linked flights into Niger between January 2025 and July 2026, with Burkina Faso as the hub. Six flights of leverage decided a capital, which is remarkably cheap - and it is also the reason to doubt it scales. The historical pattern for praetorian guarantees is that they hold until the guarantor is asked to defend the palace and the frontline in the same season, and the grievance driving this mutiny was the frontline.

angles.effect: Survives, and visibly owes the survival to a foreign detachment. A junta that needed outside help against its own soldiers has told every faction exactly where the pressure point is.

Converts a small advisory presence into a debt it can price later, and buys the strongest possible advertisement to other Sahel governments. It also now owns the outcome of the next mutiny, which is the part that is not free.

angles.party: The units from Ouallam, Tera and Dosso
angles.effect: Pay directly. The formations absorbing the worst casualties are the ones now counted among the dozens killed or arrested, and their grievance - losing the war - is untouched by the outcome.

angles.party: ECOWAS and the departed Western partners
angles.effect: Lose the last of a position. The base they built is now the platform from which a rival power stabilised the government that expelled them.

dec.kill: A visible burst of Flight Unit 224 or Il-76 traffic into Niamey above the six-flight run rate would mean the guarantee is converting into a garrison, and this read hardens. Flat airlift with the junta still standing in a month would mean the assistance was small, local and mostly political.

brief.h: The toll from Friday’s strike on a warehouse west of Kyiv reached 38, the deadliest single Russian attack of the year
brief.t: President Zelenskyy said on Sunday that the death toll from Friday night’s strike on a warehouse in the village of Myla, west of Kyiv, had risen to 38 with four people still missing and 20 injured, including two children. Ukrainian officials said the warehouse was storing ammunition; the secondary explosions and fires it set swept through dozens of nearby homes and buildings. Emergency crews were still extinguishing fires and clearing unexploded ordnance at the site on Sunday. Russia has sharply intensified its air campaign in recent weeks, with repeated alerts over Kyiv.
brief.context: This is where the week’s lesson gets tested. Robert Pape’s distinction is between denial - destroying an opponent’s physical ability to execute its strategy - and punishment, hurting a population until it presses its government. A munitions warehouse is a denial target by definition, and on the reported facts most of the 38 dead were killed not by the warhead but by what the warehouse contained. That makes this a siting outcome as much as a targeting one, and the deciding desk is doubled: a Ukrainian logistics staff that disperses stocks into settlements because concentrated depots get destroyed, and a Russian targeting cell that knows dispersal is what it is shooting into. Both halves are rational and the residents of Myla chose neither. The base rate is unkind - dispersal into inhabited areas is standard practice for an army under sustained deep strike, so this class of casualty event recurs for as long as the air campaign does, and it does not require anyone to have aimed at a house.

angles.effect: Gets a genuine logistics kill it can present two ways at once - a lawful military target for foreign audiences, and a demonstration to Ukrainians that no settlement near a depot is safe.
Loses stocks and then loses the argument about them. Confirming the site held ammunition is honest and immediately becomes the hostile talking point, which is the trap dispersal creates.
Pay everything and decided nothing. They lived next to a logistics choice made in a war ministry and were consulted about neither the storage nor the strike.
Pay in replacement stock and in political friction, since each such event makes the case for storing donated munitions near towns harder to defend at home.

dec.kill: Independent confirmation of secondary detonations consistent with stored munitions supports the denial read. Credible evidence that the site held no ordnance, or that the aimpoint was residential, moves this to punishment - and by Pape’s own record would then predict less Ukrainian concession, not more.

brief.h: Nepal began mass burials at Devghat with the toll near 800, and 898 hydropower workers are unaccounted for
brief.t: Mass burials began on Sunday at Devghat in Chitwan district, after DNA samples were taken from the bodies. The confirmed toll is approaching 800 and an estimated 898 workers across hydropower projects are unaccounted for, of whom more than 100 are believed possibly alive inside tunnels. Rescue entered a fifth day hampered by heavy overnight rain and rising rivers; the energy ministry has moved in heavy machinery and completed four boreholes, with preparations to enter a tunnel directly. The missing include large numbers of foreign nationals - about 320 Indians, roughly 100 Chinese, 62 Ukrainians, 51 Malaysians, 41 Australians, 33 Britons and 30 Canadians.
brief.context: The reason a flash flood in a Himalayan valley produces a missing list with a dozen nationalities on it is not the flood. Run-of-river hydropower in Nepal is built by imported tunnelling crews on contractor payrolls, which is why the casualty concentration is underground and why the consular problem is immediately regional. Keep the two numbers apart, because the coverage will not: the confirmed toll counts bodies, the 898 counts people not yet located, and adding them produces a figure that describes nothing. The deciding desk is Nepal’s energy ministry, which owns both the rescue and the approvals for the projects being rescued - a conflict that will matter once the inquiry starts. The base rate on tunnel entrapment is brutal but not hopeless: survival past the first week turns almost entirely on an air pocket and a drilled supply hole, which is why those four boreholes, rather than the burials, are the actual news today.

lesson: Robert Pape's Bombing to Win examined every major strategic air campaign of the twentieth century and found a hard split. Punishment - hurting a population or an economy until the pain becomes unbearable - almost never produces political concessions, because states absorb suffering far better than planners assume and civilians cannot surrender on a government's behalf. Denial - destroying the enemy's physical ability to execute its military strategy - sometimes does work, because it changes what an army can actually do tomorrow rather than how a nation feels about it. Apply that to this weekend: Ukraine's drone campaign against Russian refineries is denial, since it starves the diesel that moves an army and the export earnings that fund it, and the evidence is Russian refinery runs at a 24-year low with most fuel exports banned to keep domestic pumps full. Russia's announced campaign against Ukraine's electricity grid is punishment - it will impose enormous civilian misery through a winter and has, on the historical record, a poor conversion rate into concessions at a negotiating table. The falsifiable prediction that follows: over the next six months expect Russia's fuel constraint to shape its behaviour more than Ukraine's blackouts shape Kyiv's, and if instead Ukraine's negotiating position visibly softens under grid attack while Russia's does not under fuel shortage, Pape's distinction is failing here and we should say so.

lecture.title: The Economic Weapon: Why Sieges Make the Wars They Mean to Prevent

sections.t: Treasury designated roughly sixty Chinese “teapot” refiners — the small plants buying discounted Iranian crude — while touching no Chinese state major and no bank. The same week, central banks bought a record 288.9 tonnes of gold in the quarter gold fell over 20%. Two stories, one machine.

sections.h: Follow the money, name the mechanism
sections.t: A reserve manager buying into a 20% drawdown is not trading. He is hedging ACCESS — the risk that an asset held abroad gets switched off by its host government — and gold is the only large reserve asset with no counterparty who can flip that switch. Name the mechanism: the ECONOMIC WEAPON, using the financial plumbing whose hubs one country owns to inflict a siege without laying one. Iran discounts crude to Chinese teapots paying through dollar-touching chains; Treasury designates them; the IRGC's Strait Authority recoups the shortfall in Hormuz tolls. Sanction and gold bar are one transaction seen from two ends.

sections.h: Deep history I — the blockade that became an idea
sections.t: The economic weapon has a birthday and a founding failure. The birthday is November 1806, when Napoleon's Berlin Decrees declared the British Isles blockaded — the Continental System, an attempt to beat a maritime power by closing a continent's markets to it. It succeeded at nothing except generating enforcement. Portugal would not comply, so France invaded in 1807 and got the Peninsular War, the ulcer that bled the Grande Armée for six years. Alexander I quit the system in December 1810 because it was ruining Russian trade, and in 1812 Napoleon marched east to enforce it. The blockade never defeated Britain; it manufactured the two wars that destroyed the blockader. Sanctions require enforcement, and enforcement against a determined leakage path tends toward conquest. The second case mattered because it worked. The Allied blockade of Germany ran from 1914 through the armistice and was lifted only when Germany signed at Versailles in June 1919. German official estimates put civilian deaths from malnutrition near 424,000 — contested, and historians still argue how much was blockade and how much German agricultural mismanagement. But perception makes policy, and a generation concluded hunger had beaten an undefeated army. So they institutionalized it as a PEACE instrument: Article 16 of the League Covenant made sanctions automatic against an aggressor, and Wilson in 1919 put it in words no Treasury official would dare use today — “A nation that is boycotted is a nation that is in sight of surrender. Apply this economic, peaceful, silent, deadly remedy and there will be no need for force.” The weapon was invented to ABOLISH war; the rest of the century refutes that sentence.

sections.h: Deep history II — the failures that define our problem
sections.t: ABYSSINIA, 1935. Italy invaded Ethiopia; the League invoked Article 16 — exempting oil, coal and steel, and never closing the Suez Canal, which Britain controlled and through which Italian troopships sailed. Mussolini won anyway. The sanctions were real enough to enrage and too porous to stop, and the lesson is sharper than “sanctions don't work”: a sanction calibrated to spare the sender teaches the target that the sender is deterred too. Then the second-order effect. Nicholas Mulder's argument in The Economic Weapon is that the interwar regime deterred small states and PROVOKED large ones. Italy, Germany and Japan drew the same conclusion from the 1930s — dependence on seaborne trade was a vulnerability an enemy could switch off at will, and the answer was autarky, self-sufficiency taken by force. Lebensraum and the Co-Prosperity Sphere were ideological projects; they were also sanctions-proofing programs. Japan is the proof case. Washington embargoed scrap iron in 1940, then froze Japanese assets on 26 July 1941; America supplied roughly 80% of Japan's oil, and with Britain and the Dutch East Indies following, Japan lost about 88% of its oil imports. Reserves would last three years at peace, half that at war — Nagano's image was of a patient wasting away, every month of compliance leaving Japan weaker against the enemy it expected to fight. Pearl Harbor came in December. And the detail that turns story into discipline: the freeze was never meant to be total. Roosevelt intended a licensing regime keeping oil flowing so the tap stayed usable as leverage; officials in State and Treasury administered it so strictly that no licences issued and the flow stopped. The sanction that helped produce Pearl Harbor was substantially an organizational outcome, not a presidential decision — Allison's Essence of Decision, live. Before inferring “Iran's strategy” from one action, ask which bureau took it.

sections.h: The pattern — and where it breaks
sections.t: The leakage path is always the whole story — not the designation list, the leak: Portugal and Russia in 1806, Beira and Pretoria in 1966, Chinese teapots now. NOW THE BREAK. Japan in 1941 had a military option that promised to SOLVE its resource problem: seize the Dutch East Indies and own the oil. Iran has none — it fought its war, lost the conventional exchange, and has played its asymmetric card, the Hormuz toll. Nor did 1914 face an alternative supplier: Iran's is the world's second-largest economy, which the sanctioner just spared. Less Pearl Harbor, more Rhodesia.

MULDER says the siege provokes: strangulation drives large states to autarky, then preemption. DREZNER says sanctions are cheap theater — Hufbauer's data give a third success rate at best, near zero against great powers. The 2026 evidence buries neither: it splits by SIDE, and the split is the finding. On the TARGET Mulder scores: gold, stockpiles, payment rails, enrichment acceleration under maximum pressure. On the SENDER Drezner scores harder — the carve-outs. Sixty teapots and not one bank is not escalation; it is the sanctioner taking its own threat hostage, because hitting a Chinese bank endangers the dollar system that makes the hammer heavy.

The 2015 architecture is not coming back (high confidence): the 2022 freeze of Russian reserves turned the settlement network into an instrument; a hedge once bought is not resold. Expect bifurcation, not de-dollarization (moderate-high). EICHENGREEN is right that currencies erode glacially; the WEAPON depreciates faster than the CURRENCY. The bolder call (moderate): the most dangerous decade is the one in which the weapon still works but no longer terrifies. Mulder's mechanism fires in the transition — invested in escaping, not finished, expecting strangulation regardless. For China, the 2030s — so Economic D-Day may SHORTEN the fuse it was meant to lengthen. FALSIFIER: designate a major Chinese state bank; if Beijing cuts Iranian purchases within a quarter, I am wrong. Two centuries say the economic weapon does not replace war — it sorts the world into blocs that survive each other's sieges, then gives the survivors a reason to fight.

Nicholas Mulder, The Economic Weapon (2022) — published weeks before the Russia sanctions matched its template. Farrell & Newman, “Weaponized Interdependence” (2019) — it called the 2022 playbook and the chip controls in advance. Eichengreen, Exorbitant Privilege — the counterweight.
